opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, because it gets at what the web is actually for, and what changes when the reader is increasingly an AI agent instead of a person.

The SEC filing is the source of truth. It's authoritative, it's legally accountable, and it's complete. But it's also long and dense, and it's written for compliance rather than comprehension. So for a long time the repackaging layer did real work. It pulled out the five numbers you cared about, put them next to last quarter's, maybe added some context or an analyst's take. That was useful for a human with ten minutes and a question.

The question I keep coming back to is: what portion of that value was *access* and what portion was *insight*? A lot of those pages were really about access. The filing was hard to read, and the page made it easier. Then they monetized your attention with ads while you were there. When the consumer is an agent that can read a 10-K in seconds, the access value mostly goes away. The agent doesn't need someone to summarize the revenue line. It can go to the primary source, and it should, because every intermediate layer is another chance for a transcription error or a stale number.

What doesn't go away is genuine synthesis. That means comparing across companies, normalizing metrics that different firms report differently, original analysis, or a viewpoint that isn't in the filing at all. That's real value, and I'd argue the people creating it deserve to be paid for it, whether the reader is a person or a machine.

So my honest view is that the web is going to sort itself. Pages that were mostly rehosting public information will lose their reason to exist. Pages that add something new will become more valuable, as long as we build the right infrastructure for agents to find them, trust them, and compensate them. A lot of what I care about is making sure that second part actually happens, so that the economics of the web reward original work rather than just whoever sits closest to the reader.

r001.rationale: The response says the filing is long and dense, while repackaging pages made it easier to find useful information by pulling out key figures.

r002.rationale: It describes repackaging pages as pulling out “the five numbers you cared about,” identifying selection and emphasis of figures as added value.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends on what the reader was actually trying to do, and most of the time the authoritative filing is not what they were trying to do.

A 10-K is a legal document. It's written by lawyers and auditors for a specific regulatory purpose, and it's optimized for completeness and defensibility, not for being understood. If you're a retail investor trying to figure out whether a company's gross margin is improving, the answer is in there, but you may have to read two hundred pages and reconcile three tables to get it. So when a site pulls the numbers out, puts them in a chart, compares them to the prior four quarters, and adds two sentences of context, that's real work. It's a transformation, not just a copy. And the value of that transformation is roughly proportional to how much effort it saves the reader relative to what they'd lose in trust by not going to the source.

That said, there's a spectrum, and I'd draw the line in a few places. The first question is whether the page adds anything, or whether it's just scraping and reformatting to capture search traffic. A lot of what I saw when I was working on relevance was pages that existed purely because people search for "Apple revenue 2023" and nobody wants to click into EDGAR. Those pages are useful in a narrow sense, but they're fragile. They can be wrong, they can be stale, and they often don't tell you where the number came from. The second question is whether the page makes it easy to get back to the source. A good summary says "here's the number, here's the filing, here's the page." A bad one hides provenance because that's what keeps you on the page.

And the thing I'd push on, especially now, is that this is exactly the kind of content that models are going to generate at enormous scale. The marginal cost of producing a plausible-looking financial summary is approaching zero. So the value of the repackaging itself goes to zero too, and what's left is the trust layer: is this number right, is it current, and can I verify it in one click. I'd argue that's what ranking systems and the people building them should be rewarding. Not "did you summarize the filing" but "did you make the authoritative source more reachable, and did you take responsibility for being correct." If a page does those two things, it's genuinely valuable. If it does neither, it's noise that happens to be about finance.

r001.rationale: It says summaries can save readers from searching through a lengthy 10-K and reconciling tables to find an answer.

r002.rationale: It describes extracting numbers and presenting them in charts, but does not identify choosing which figures deserve prominence as a source of added value.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is: what are they adding? The SEC filing is the authoritative source, but it may not be the easiest way to answer a particular question. If a page helps you understand the numbers, compare them across companies, or see what changed over time, that’s useful work. It’s making public information more accessible.

If it’s simply copying the information and putting itself between you and the source, the value is much less clear. Ideally, you get both: a useful explanation and a clear path back to the filing so you can check the details. Authority and usefulness are related, but they’re not the same thing.

r001.rationale: It says the SEC filing may not be the easiest way to answer a particular question and that a page can make the numbers easier to understand, communicating reduced effort to get an answer from the authoritative source.

r002.rationale: It mentions explaining numbers, comparing companies, and showing changes over time, but does not identify choosing which figures from a lengthy report to feature prominently.

sol-6.1.text: I think the value is in what they add. The SEC filing is the authoritative source, but it isn’t necessarily the easiest way for someone to answer a particular question. A page that organizes the information, explains it, or makes it easier to compare companies can be useful. If it’s simply copying the same information without adding anything, the value is much less clear. Ideally, that layer of interpretation also makes it easy to get back to the original filing and verify what you’re reading.
